items.headline: Building a Design System from Scratch in Figma
items.background: Many designers tasked with creating an organization-wide design system face an undocumented starting problem: where to actually begin in Figma before any components or tokens exist. This case study documents one designer's live process rather than a polished retrospective.
keyFindings: Author started with foundational decisions (color tokens, type scales) before building components, not the other way around
Building for an entire organization required negotiating with stakeholders on naming conventions and component scope early
Snippet cuts off before key learnings are revealed, limiting what can be confirmed from the piece
items.implications: Useful as a process reference for designers starting a system with no prior foundation, but the Medium paywall/truncation means core lessons aren't fully accessible. Treat as a starting-point reference, not a complete guide.

items.headline: Building a Design System from Scratch in Figma (Spanish)
items.background: This appears to be a direct Spanish-language translation or parallel version of article #1, targeting Spanish-speaking UX practitioners with the same Figma design system case study content.
keyFindings: Content mirrors the English version: org-wide design system built from scratch in Figma
Published separately on Medium, suggesting intentional localization for Spanish-speaking audience
No additional findings distinguishable from the English version based on available snippet
items.implications: Relevant if you're sourcing materials for Spanish-speaking team members or running multilingual design training. No distinct new information beyond the English version.

items.headline: AI Skills for UX Designers, Organized by Job Type
items.background: AI tool adoption in UX is accelerating but guidance tends to be generic — 'learn AI' advice without specificity about which skills matter for which UX roles. This piece attempts to map skills to actual job functions.
keyFindings: Skills are organized by job type rather than tool category, making it more actionable for role-specific upskilling
Includes direct links to resources for each skill area, not just a list
Covers roles including researchers, interaction designers, and content strategists separately
items.implications: More useful than generic AI listicles because it maps to specific UX job functions. Relevant for hiring managers defining role requirements and for individual designers building a focused learning plan.

items.headline: Does Gamma Actually Replace PowerPoint and Figma for Presentations?
items.background: AI presentation tools like Gamma are being adopted by product teams as faster alternatives to Figma for stakeholder decks and PowerPoint for slide-based communication. The question is whether speed comes at the cost of design control or fidelity.
keyFindings: Snippet and content not available — no substantive claims can be confirmed from this piece
Gamma uses AI to auto-generate slide layouts from prompts or outlines
The comparison involves two very different tools: PowerPoint (presentation delivery) and Figma (design fidelity), suggesting Gamma occupies a middle-use-case niche
items.implications: Worth investigating if your team spends significant time on stakeholder presentations, but be cautious about replacing Figma for anything requiring precise layout or design-system-aligned visuals. No findings available to confirm the article's conclusions.

items.headline: Digital Health Design Is Failing Women Who Need It Most
items.background: Women's health apps and digital health platforms have grown rapidly, but critics argue they are disproportionately designed around affluent, tech-literate users — leaving out women with lower digital literacy, chronic conditions, or limited access to devices.
keyFindings: Piece focuses on underserved women as the primary design target, not as an afterthought or edge case
Raises access and literacy barriers as design problems, not just infrastructure problems
Published in Punch Newspapers, suggesting a Sub-Saharan African regional perspective on the issue
items.implications: Designers working on health platforms should audit assumptions about baseline digital literacy and device access in their user research. This applies especially to teams expanding into emerging markets or designing for older or lower-income demographics.

items.headline: Why Federal Digital Services Must Be Built on Evidence
items.background: Government digital delivery has historically been driven by policy mandates and vendor proposals rather than user evidence and outcome data. This piece, from consulting firm ICF, argues for a more data-grounded approach to federal digital service design and evaluation.
keyFindings: Argues that without evidence frameworks, federal digital services risk solving the wrong problems at scale
Positions data not just as a measurement tool but as a design input throughout delivery
Source is ICF, a government consultancy — perspective is practitioner-facing but comes with inherent advocacy interest
items.implications: Relevant for anyone doing UX or product work within or alongside government agencies. The evidence-first framing aligns with USDS and 18F methodology, but readers should note ICF's commercial stake in this position.

items.headline: High-Paying Skills for Graduates in 2026: What Makes the List
items.background: Career guidance for students often lags behind actual market demand, especially in tech. This guide attempts to identify which skills command the highest salaries entering the job market in 2026, aimed at pre-graduation planning.
keyFindings: AI and machine learning skills appear alongside UX and data analysis as top earners
Guide targets students about to enter the job market, not mid-career professionals
Published in Youth Incorporated Magazine — audience is students, framing is aspirational rather than rigorous
items.implications: Limited direct value for working UX professionals. Useful context if you're hiring new graduates or advising students on where to focus. Treat salary claims as directional, not precise, given the publication's general-audience nature.

items.headline: Profile: How Kait Hines Is Shaping Human-Centered UX Practice
items.background: Profiles of individual UX practitioners are increasingly common as the field grows, often serving to highlight emerging methodologies or institutional approaches through personal narratives.
keyFindings: Hines is highlighted for applying human-centered design principles in her organizational UX work
Published via EIN News wire, which typically distributes PR-originated content — editorial independence is limited
No specific methodologies, tools, or case data are cited in the available snippet
items.implications: Minimal practical takeaway for working practitioners. May be worth reading for context on how human-centered design is being positioned institutionally, but approach as a profile piece rather than a technical resource.

items.headline: Teague's VP of Design on HCD for Complex Physical Systems
items.background: Human-centered design methodology is well-documented for software and digital products, but its application to complex physical systems — aerospace, industrial equipment, transportation — is less visible in mainstream UX discourse. Teague is a design firm with deep roots in exactly this space.
keyFindings: Matt McElvogue discusses applying HCD to physical systems where failure consequences are high and iteration cycles are long
Teague's work spans aviation and transportation, where UX decisions affect safety, not just satisfaction
Interview format means findings are qualitative and practitioner-perspective, not research-based
items.implications: Valuable for UX designers working in hardware, industrial, or safety-critical product domains who rarely see their context represented in mainstream UX content. Less directly applicable to purely digital product teams.

items.headline: Discuss Launches AI Tool to Analyze Entire Research Libraries
items.background: Research operations teams accumulate large archives of user research that often go underutilized because synthesis across studies is time-consuming. Discuss, a qualitative research platform, has released a tool aimed at querying and analyzing across an organization's full research library.
keyFindings: The tool allows researchers to run analysis queries across multiple past studies simultaneously, not just individual sessions
Targets the specific pain point of institutional research going unused due to synthesis overhead
Discuss positions this as a research operations feature, suggesting it's aimed at teams with substantial existing research archives rather than new research programs
items.implications: Directly relevant for UX research teams building or scaling a research repository. Most valuable if your organization already has significant qualitative research volume in Discuss; limited utility otherwise. Evaluate carefully how the tool handles synthesis accuracy before relying on it for strategic decisions.
